quiz.question: Two countries trade grain for cloth. Cloth costs one of them 2 grain to make and the other 1 grain. Which exchange rate leaves both better off?
options: 0.8 grain per cloth
2.4 grain per cloth
Any rate at all, provided both countries agree to it
1.5 grain per cloth
quiz.explanation: The rate has to sit strictly between the two domestic costs. Below 1 the low-cost producer would rather keep making its own; above 2 the other would. 1.50 is inside the range, so both gain.

quiz.question: Which of these is a LIMITATION of the theory of comparative advantage rather than an assumption of it?
options: Resources move freely between industries at no cost and no delay
There are two countries and two goods, and nothing else exists
Transport costs can exhaust the predicted gain
Opportunity costs stay constant however far specialisation goes
quiz.explanation: The other three are assumptions the model makes to get its result. Transport costs exhausting the gain is what happens when one of those assumptions is relaxed, which is what a limitation is.

quiz.question: Emerging economies' share of world exports rose from 24% to 44%. What happened to the advanced economies' share?
options: It fell to 56%
It fell to 24%
It stayed the same
It cannot be determined
quiz.explanation: Shares sum to 100%, so a rise of 20% points on one side is a fall of 20% on the other: 76% to 56%. A falling share is not the same as falling exports, because the world total moved too.

quiz.question: Kalto doubles its grain capacity to 80, leaving cloth at 40. What happens to trade with Merida?
options: Kalto now has a comparative advantage in both goods
Trade continues between them at the same exchange rate as before
Merida gains a comparative advantage in cloth
The basis for trade between them disappears
quiz.explanation: Cloth now costs Kalto 2 grain, which is exactly what it costs Merida. Identical opportunity costs mean neither country has a comparative advantage in anything, so there is no gain left to divide. A country cannot have a comparative advantage in both goods; the ratios are reciprocals.

quiz.question: A currency falls from 2 foreign units per domestic unit to 1.60. A good priced 100 at home now sells abroad for:
quiz.explanation: 100 × 1.60 = 160, down from 100 × 2 = 200. Exports become cheaper abroad when the currency falls, which is why the pattern of trade shifts towards them.

quiz.question: A government puts a duty on tiles imported from ONE country. Which outcome is the one students most often miss?
options: Domestic tile makers raise their output
The domestic price of tiles rises
An exporter in a third country takes the business
Imports of tiles from that country fall
quiz.explanation: The first, second and fourth are the intended effects and are usually stated. Because the measure named a country rather than a good, much of the demand moves to the nearest supplier the duty does not cover rather than home — so total imports fall by less than the measure suggests.

quiz.question: An economy's exports grow from $80.0bn to $100.0bn. Ore falls from 70% of them to 40%. What happened to the VALUE of ore exports?
options: It fell to $40.0bn
It rose to $40.0bn
It fell to $24.0bn
It cannot be worked out
quiz.explanation: 70% of $80.0bn is $56.0bn; 40% of $100.0bn is $40.0bn. Here both the share and the value fell — but they need not: a smaller share of a much larger total can be worth more.

quiz.question: The terms of trade are best described as:
options: The difference between export and import values
The ratio of export prices to import prices
The volume of exports divided by the volume of imports
The balance of trade expressed as an index
quiz.explanation: They are a ratio of two PRICE indices. The difference between export and import values is the balance of trade, which is a different figure that can move the other way in the same year.

quiz.question: Sarova's export price index is 120 and its import price index is 110. Its terms of trade are:
quiz.explanation: 120 ÷ 110 × 100 = 109.1, an improvement on the base of 100.0. Note that BOTH prices rose: the ratio improved because exports rose faster, not because imports got cheaper.

quiz.question: A country's inflation rate is higher than its trading partners'. Its terms of trade:
options: Deteriorate, because the country has become less competitive abroad
Are unchanged, because inflation affects both indices equally
Cannot be predicted from this information alone
Improve, because export prices rise faster
quiz.explanation: Domestic inflation raises the export price index faster than foreign inflation raises the import price index, so the ratio rises. Competitiveness falls at the same time — the two move in opposite directions, which is why an improvement is a direction and not a verdict.

quiz.question: Which cause of a DETERIORATION in the terms of trade is a sign of economic strength?
options: The world price of the single export commodity collapsed
Rising productivity allowed export prices to be cut
The price of essential imported fuel doubled
The currency fell after capital left the country
quiz.explanation: All four lower the ratio. Only the second does it by lowering costs, which almost certainly means larger volumes and higher earnings. What moved the ratio decides what the movement means.

quiz.question: A currency rises sharply. What happens to the two price indices behind the terms of trade?
options: The export index falls and the import index rises
Both indices rise together, so the ratio between them is unchanged
Neither index moves until firms decide to change their prices
The export index rises and the import index falls
quiz.explanation: Measured in foreign currency, a stronger currency makes exports dearer; measured at home, it makes imports cheaper. A larger number over a smaller one, so the terms of trade improve — before any firm has changed a price list.

quiz.question: Sarova's export prices rose 20% and volume fell 30%. Its export revenue index is:
quiz.explanation: Revenue is price times quantity: 1.20 × 0.70 = 0.84, an index of 84. The terms of trade improved to 109.1 and revenue fell by 16% — both are true.

quiz.question: An improvement in the terms of trade RAISES export revenue when demand for exports is:
options: Elastic
Unitary
Perfectly elastic
Inelastic
quiz.explanation: With inelastic demand the quantity falls by proportionally less than the price rose, so revenue rises. With elastic demand the quantity effect wins and revenue falls. Unitary leaves revenue unchanged, and perfectly elastic means no sales at all at the higher price.

quiz.question: Sarova's terms of trade improved to 109.1 and its trade moved from balance to a deficit of $13.0bn. This is:
options: A contradiction, so one of the figures must be wrong
Only possible if import volumes also rose
What elastic export demand produces
Evidence that the terms of trade were miscalculated
quiz.explanation: Export earnings fell to $42.0bn because volume fell more than price rose, while the same quantity of imports cost $55.0bn at the higher import prices. A price ratio and a difference of values are not required to agree.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest basis for judging a change in the terms of trade?
options: Whether the index rose or fell
Whether the change was large
What caused it, and how responsive demand is
Whether the balance of trade moved with it
quiz.explanation: Direction alone is the rule the exam is built to punish: a deterioration from rising productivity is good news and an improvement from an over-strong currency is not. Cause and elasticity are what decide, and a judgement carrying both is what Evaluate asks for.

options: The tariff revenue collected by the government
The increase in producer surplus for domestic steel firms
The domestic production of steel at a higher cost than the world price
The rise in the domestic price of steel
quiz.question: A government imposes a tariff on imported steel. Which of the following is a welfare loss from the tariff?
quiz.explanation: A welfare loss from a tariff occurs because domestic firms now produce units of steel that could have been imported at a lower world price — this is production inefficiency. Resources are wasted producing domestically what could be imported more cheaply. Government revenue and producer surplus are transfers (redistributed from consumers), not welfare losses. The price rise itself is not a loss but the mechanism through which the other effects occur.

options: The industry has been established for decades but faces foreign competition
The domestic industry has potential to achieve economies of scale and become internationally competitive, and protection is temporary
The industry provides goods essential for national security
Foreign producers are dumping goods below cost
quiz.question: The infant industry argument for protectionism is strongest when:
quiz.explanation: The infant industry argument states that new domestic industries may need temporary protection from established foreign competitors while they grow, develop economies of scale, and gain experience. The argument is strongest when there is genuine potential for the industry to become competitive AND protection is strictly temporary. Option A describes a geriatric (declining) industry. Options C and D are valid reasons for protection but are separate arguments from the infant industry case.

options: National Treatment
Reciprocity
Most Favoured Nation (MFN)
Transparency
quiz.question: Which WTO principle requires that any trade concession given to one member must be extended to all members?
quiz.explanation: The Most Favoured Nation (MFN) principle is the cornerstone WTO rule that members must treat all trading partners equally — any tariff reduction or trade concession given to one WTO member must be automatically extended to all other members. National Treatment means imported goods must be treated equally to domestic goods once inside the market. Reciprocity means trade liberalisation should be mutual. Transparency means trade policies must be published and predictable.

options: A quota generates government revenue whereas a tariff does not
A quota creates quota rent for licence holders instead of government revenue
A quota does not raise the domestic price above the world price
A quota benefits consumers more than a tariff
quiz.question: How does a quota differ from a tariff in its welfare effects?
quiz.explanation: The key difference is that a tariff generates government revenue (area c in the tariff diagram), whereas a quota creates quota rent — an economic surplus that goes to whoever holds the import licences (which may be foreign exporters). Both raise the domestic price, both harm consumers, and both create welfare losses. Quotas are generally considered worse than tariffs because no revenue is generated for the government and they are less transparent.

options: A 15% ad valorem tariff on imported electronics
A quota limiting car imports to 50,000 units per year
Requiring imported food products to meet extremely strict labelling and safety standards that are difficult for foreign producers to comply with
A government subsidy to domestic car manufacturers
quiz.question: Which of the following is the best example of a non-tariff barrier to trade?
quiz.explanation: Non-tariff barriers (NTBs) are regulatory and administrative measures that restrict trade without being tariffs or quotas. Strict product standards, labelling requirements, and safety regulations that foreign producers find difficult to comply with are classic examples of NTBs. Option A is a tariff, option B is a quota (a quantitative restriction), and option D is a subsidy — none of these are non-tariff barriers in the strict sense.

practice.question: Define the term 'comparative advantage'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two marks, so two things have to be in the sentence. Appendix 6 defines Define as knowledge and understanding only: no example, no development, no diagram. Write the definition, then check it against the trap below.

The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country (1 mark). Opportunity cost is the amount of the other good given up to produce it (1 mark). A definition resting on producing MORE has defined absolute advantage and earns nothing.

practice.question: A country's export price index rises from 100 to 126 while its import price index rises from 100 to 105. Calculate its terms of trade and state whether they have improved or deteriorated. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Four marks for a calculation in stages, so set the formula down first and work through it on the page. Appendix 6 advises showing workings, and an unsupported final figure cannot be given method marks. The last mark is for the word the question asks for, not the number.

Terms of trade = export price index ÷ import price index × 100 (1 mark). 126 ÷ 105 = 1.2 (1 mark). × 100 = 120.0 (1 mark). Above the base of 100, so the terms of trade have improved (1 mark). Note that both indices rose: exports simply rose faster.

practice.question: Explain two factors that may cause a deterioration in a country's terms of trade. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two factors, two marks each, and the marks are in the chain rather than the naming. Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring a two-stage chain for a reason or an impact: the factor, then how it reaches one of the two price indices, then what that does to the ratio. Pick from the five the specification lists.

Available: a rise in relative productivity that lowers export prices; a fall in the exchange rate, which lowers the export index and raises the import index at once; relative labour costs rising more slowly than abroad; relative inflation below trading partners'; or a fall in the world price of the goods exported.

practice.question: Analyse two factors that may change the pattern of trade between countries. (6 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two factors, three marks each, and each has to reach a named flow — which goods, moving in which direction, between whom. Appendix 6 defines Analyse as a developed chain of reasoning, so a list of the specification's five factors is not an answer however complete the list is.

Available: the growth of emerging economies; changes in comparative advantage, which can remove a basis for trade entirely when opportunity costs converge; the growth of trading blocs and bilateral agreements, which redirect purchases towards members; changes in relative exchange rates; changes in protectionism, which can send trade home OR to an uncovered third country.

practice.question: Examine the impact of an improvement in a country's terms of trade on its export revenues and its balance of trade. (8 marks)
practice.guidance:
Eight marks, and the question names two things to examine — take them in turn rather than together. Appendix 6 requires analysis as well as application, so each one needs the mechanism and then a number from the extract applied to it. The second effect is the one most answers never reach.

The mechanism first: an improvement means export prices rose relative to import prices, so each unit of exports earns more and buys more imports. Then the volume response, which is where the marks are: with elastic export demand, quantity falls proportionally more than price rose and export revenue falls. Apply it — a 20% price rise with an elasticity of 1.5 gives a 30% volume fall and a revenue index of 84. The balance of trade can then move into deficit even though the ratio improved, because import spending rose while export earnings fell.

practice.question: Evaluate the view that specialisation and free trade always raise a country's living standards. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Twenty marks, and the word doing the work in the question is ALWAYS. Build both sides, then make the judgement conditional: on the terms of trade this economy faces, on how diversified it is, and on whether displaced resources can move. A confident verdict with no conditions attached is what this question is designed to separate out.

In support: total output rises where countries specialise by comparative advantage; economies of scale lower unit costs; consumers gain lower prices and wider choice; the purchasing power of a unit of exports can rise. Against: the gain depends on the exchange rate that splits it, and a rate near one country's own opportunity cost gives it almost nothing; transport costs and rising costs of production erode the predicted gain; specialisation concentrates risk, so a fall in one export price can be severe; and workers in industries that close bear a cost the national total conceals.

Effect 1: Higher prices for consumers (1 mark) — a tariff is a tax on imports that raises the price of the imported good above the world price, reducing consumer surplus (1 mark). Domestic consumers pay more and consume less, leading to a welfare loss (1 mark).

Effect 2: Protection of domestic producers (1 mark) — the higher import price allows domestic firms to increase output because they become more price-competitive relative to imports (1 mark). However, this can lead to productive inefficiency as firms face less competitive pressure to minimise costs (1 mark).
practice.question: Explain two economic effects of imposing a tariff on imported goods. (6 marks)

practice.guidance:
Introduction: Define free trade as the absence of government-imposed barriers to international trade, and protectionism as the use of tariffs, quotas and other measures to restrict imports (2 marks).

For free trade: Comparative advantage — specialisation according to comparative advantage increases world output and allows countries to consume beyond their PPF (3 marks); lower prices and greater choice for consumers through access to global markets (2 marks); competitive pressure drives innovation and efficiency among domestic firms (2 marks).

Against — arguments for protectionism: Infant industry argument — new industries in developing countries may need temporary protection from established foreign competitors until they achieve economies of scale (3 marks); protection of strategic industries — countries may wish to maintain domestic capacity in defence or food production for national security (2 marks); anti-dumping measures — protection may be justified when foreign firms sell below cost to destroy domestic competition (2 marks).

Evaluation: Free trade generally increases global welfare, but 'always preferable' is too strong (2 marks). Temporary, targeted protectionism may be justified in specific circumstances, but the risk of government failure — protection becoming permanent due to political lobbying — and retaliation from trading partners means protectionism should be used cautiously and sparingly (2 marks).
practice.question: Evaluate the view that free trade is always preferable to protectionism. (20 marks)

flashcards.front: What is specialisation in an international context?
flashcards.back: Concentrating a country's resources on a narrower range of goods than it consumes, and trading for the rest.

flashcards.front: What is absolute advantage?
flashcards.back: Producing more of a good from the same resources than another country can. It decides nothing on its own.

flashcards.front: What is comparative advantage?
flashcards.back: Producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country. A country can have an absolute advantage in everything and a comparative advantage in only some things.

flashcards.front: How is opportunity cost worked out from a production table?
flashcards.back: Divide one maximum by the other. Merida can make 120 grain or 60 cloth, so one cloth costs 2 grain.

flashcards.front: Why does partial specialisation show the gain more clearly than complete specialisation?
flashcards.back: Because one good can be held constant. Here cloth stays at 50 and grain rises from 80 to 100 — a gain with nothing given up.

flashcards.front: What limits the exchange rate between two traded goods?
flashcards.back: It must lie strictly between the two countries' own opportunity costs — here between 1 and 2 grain per cloth — or one of them refuses to trade.

flashcards.front: What are the four assumptions behind comparative advantage?
flashcards.back: Constant opportunity costs; perfect factor mobility; no transport costs or barriers; two countries and two goods, fully employed.

flashcards.front: What are the main limitations of the theory?
flashcards.back: Costs rise as a country specialises; advantage can be created and lost; transport costs eat the gain; and the theory predicts the total gain, not how it is split or who bears the adjustment.

flashcards.front: What is a pattern of trade?
flashcards.back: The composition of trade — which goods, with which partners, in what proportions. Distinct from volume, which is how much.

flashcards.front: What five factors influence patterns of trade?
flashcards.back: Emerging economies; changes in comparative advantage; growth in trading blocs and bilateral trading agreements; changes in relative exchange rates; changes in protectionism.

flashcards.front: What is an emerging economy?
flashcards.back: An economy growing quickly from a low base, industrialising, and taking a rising share of world output and trade.

flashcards.front: Why can a country's export share fall while its exports rise?
flashcards.back: Because a share is a proportion of a moving total. On a world total that has doubled, a smaller share can still be worth more.

flashcards.front: How does a falling currency change trade prices?
flashcards.back: Exports become cheaper abroad (200 → 160) and imports dearer at home (100 → 125).

flashcards.front: What are the terms of trade?
flashcards.back: The rate at which exports exchange for imports: the export price index ÷ import price index × 100. A ratio of prices, not of values or volumes.

flashcards.front: How are the terms of trade calculated?
flashcards.back: Divide the export price index by the import price index and multiply by 100. 120 ÷ 110 × 100 = 109.1.

flashcards.front: What does an IMPROVEMENT in the terms of trade mean?
flashcards.back: The ratio has risen: each unit of exports commands more imports. It is a direction, not a verdict — it can coincide with falling revenue.

flashcards.front: What five factors influence the terms of trade?
flashcards.back: Relative inflation rates; relative productivity rates; relative labour costs; the exchange rate; and the prices of imports and exports.

flashcards.front: Why does higher domestic inflation IMPROVE the terms of trade?
flashcards.back: It pushes the export price index up faster than the import price index, so the ratio rises — while competitiveness falls at the same time.

flashcards.front: Why can a deterioration be a sign of strength?
flashcards.back: If rising productivity cut unit costs and export prices, the country sells more cheaply from a stronger position and is likely to sell more.

flashcards.front: What decides whether an improvement raises export revenue?
flashcards.back: The price elasticity of demand for exports. Elastic demand means revenue falls; inelastic means it rises. At 1.50, Sarova's revenue index fell to 84.

flashcards.front: What is the balance of trade?
flashcards.back: The value of exports minus the value of imports. It can worsen in the same year the terms of trade improve.

flashcards.front: How should a change in the terms of trade be judged?
flashcards.back: By asking what caused it and how responsive demand is — never by the direction of the index alone.
Countries agree to eliminate tariffs between members but maintain individual external tariffs with non-members. E.g., NAFTA/USMCA.
flashcards.front: What is a free trade area?

flashcards.back: A free trade area with a common external tariff applied to all non-member imports. E.g., the EU's customs union.
flashcards.front: What is a customs union?

flashcards.back: When a trade bloc replaces high-cost domestic production with lower-cost imports from a member country. Increases efficiency and consumer welfare.
flashcards.front: What is trade creation?

flashcards.back: When a trade bloc diverts imports from a lower-cost non-member to a higher-cost member. Reduces efficiency — the external tariff makes non-member goods artificially expensive.
flashcards.front: What is trade diversion?

flashcards.back: Trade without government-imposed barriers (tariffs, quotas, regulations). Allows countries to specialise according to comparative advantage, increasing global output.
flashcards.front: What is free trade?

flashcards.back: A tax on imports that raises the price of foreign goods. Protects domestic firms but raises prices for consumers and may provoke retaliation.
flashcards.front: What is a tariff?

flashcards.back: A physical limit on the quantity of imports allowed into a country. Restricts foreign competition but reduces consumer choice and raises prices.
flashcards.front: What is a quota?

flashcards.back: Government policies that restrict international trade to protect domestic industries — through tariffs, quotas, subsidies, or regulations. Reduces competition but may harm consumers.
flashcards.front: What is protectionism?

flashcards.back: Protecting infant industries, preventing dumping (selling below cost), and maintaining national security (strategic industries like defence or food production).
flashcards.front: Name three arguments for protectionism.

flashcards.back: Raises consumer prices, reduces choice and efficiency, may provoke trade wars (retaliation), and protects inefficient firms from competition.
flashcards.front: Name three arguments against protectionism.

flashcards.back: Selling exports at a price below the cost of production in the foreign market. Used to gain market share or dispose of surplus. Can destroy domestic industries in the importing country.
flashcards.front: What is dumping?

flashcards.back: New industries in developing countries need temporary protection from established foreign competitors until they achieve economies of scale and can compete independently.
flashcards.front: What is an infant industry argument?

flashcards.back: A government payment to domestic exporters to reduce their costs and make exports cheaper. A form of protectionism that distorts trade. Banned under WTO rules in most cases.
flashcards.front: What is an export subsidy?

flashcards.back: Any trade restriction that is not a tariff — e.g., quotas, regulations, licensing, safety standards, bureaucratic delays. Often harder to identify and challenge than tariffs.
flashcards.front: What is a non-tariff barrier?

diagrams.title: The Effect of a Tariff (Welfare Analysis)
checklist: Draw domestic supply (upward) and demand (downward) curves with correctly labelled axes
Show the world price (Pw) as a horizontal line below the domestic equilibrium price
Show the tariff-inclusive price (Pw+t) as a second horizontal line above Pw
Identify Q1 to Q4: domestic supply and demand at each price level
Label and shade: producer surplus gain (a), welfare losses (b and d), government revenue (c)
State that consumer surplus loss = a + b + c + d and net welfare loss = b + d
Note that imports fall from (Q4 - Q1) to (Q3 - Q2)

scenarios.label: Free trade
scenarios.description: At world price Pw, domestic supply is Q1 and domestic demand is Q4. Imports fill the gap (Q4 - Q1). Consumer surplus is maximised.

scenarios.label: After tariff
scenarios.description: Price rises to Pw+t. Domestic supply expands to Q2, demand contracts to Q3. Imports fall to (Q3 - Q2). Consumers lose surplus, producers gain, government earns revenue, but two triangles of welfare loss remain.

diagrams.description: A supply and demand diagram showing the welfare effects of imposing a tariff on imports, including consumer surplus loss, producer surplus gain, government revenue, and the two welfare loss triangles.

diagrams.title: Types of Trading Blocs (Levels of Integration)
checklist: List the four types in order: FTA, Customs Union, Common Market, Economic/Monetary Union
Know the key distinguishing feature of each level
Provide a real-world example for each type
Understand that each level includes all features of those below it
Explain that higher integration means greater benefits but also greater loss of sovereignty

scenarios.label: Low integration (FTA)
scenarios.description: Countries remove barriers between themselves but retain sovereignty over external trade policy. Simple to negotiate but risk of trade deflection.

scenarios.label: High integration (Monetary Union)
scenarios.description: Countries share a currency and harmonise economic policies. Maximum trade benefits and lowest transaction costs, but significant loss of policy sovereignty and flexibility.

mistakes.title: Confusing absolute and comparative advantage
mistakes.mistake: Students say a country has a comparative advantage because it can produce more of a good, or produce it more cheaply.
mistakes.correction: Those are absolute statements. Comparative advantage is a ratio inside one country — what it gives up of the other good — compared across countries. Merida can make more of both goods and still has a comparative advantage in only one.
mistakes.examTip: Always compute both opportunity costs before writing anything. One division per country per good, and the lower figure decides.

mistakes.title: Specialising completely and calling the result a gain
mistakes.mistake: Students move every resource into the good each country is best at, find more of one good and less of the other, and call it a gain.
mistakes.correction: Complete specialisation here gives 120 grain and 40 cloth against 80 and 50 without trade — more grain and LESS cloth. Specialise partially so one good is held constant, and the gain is unambiguous.
mistakes.examTip: Hold one good at its no-trade level and put the rest into the other. If both goods moved, you have shown a trade-off and not a gain.

mistakes.title: Reading a falling share as a falling value
mistakes.mistake: Students see an export share drop and conclude that the country is exporting less.
mistakes.correction: A share is a proportion of a moving total. An advanced economy going from 76% to 56% of a world total that has grown can be exporting considerably more than before.
mistakes.examTip: Whenever a question gives you a share, look for the total. If the total is not given, say what the share does and do not claim anything about the value.

mistakes.title: Treating an improvement in the terms of trade as good news
mistakes.mistake: Students read "improvement" as a verdict and write that the economy is better off.
mistakes.correction: An improvement raises the purchasing power of each unit of exports and can cut export revenue and push the balance of trade into deficit at the same time. Sarova's improvement to 109.1 came with a revenue index of 84 and a deficit of $13.0bn.
mistakes.examTip: Two questions every time: what moved the ratio, and how elastic is demand for exports? An answer carrying both is doing what Evaluate asks.

mistakes.title: Confusing the terms of trade with the balance of trade
mistakes.mistake: Students use the two interchangeably, because both use the word improvement about the same country in the same year.
mistakes.correction: The terms of trade are a ratio of PRICE indices. The balance of trade is the difference between the VALUE of exports and the value of imports. Nothing forces them to move together, and in the elastic case they move apart.
mistakes.examTip: If the question gives you price indices, it is about the terms of trade. If it gives you values or an elasticity, the balance of trade is in play.

mistakes.title: Not showing welfare loss on a tariff diagram
mistakes.mistake: Students draw the tariff diagram but forget to identify and shade the welfare loss triangles.
mistakes.correction: A tariff creates TWO welfare loss triangles: one representing lost consumer surplus (production inefficiency) and one representing lost consumer surplus (consumption inefficiency). Mark both clearly.

chains.title: From an export price rise to a trade deficit
steps: Export prices rise relative to import prices, so the terms of trade improve.
Foreign buyers respond to the higher price by cutting the quantity they order.
Demand is elastic, so the fall in quantity outweighs the rise in price: at an elasticity of 1.50, a 20% rise costs 30% of the volume.
Export earnings fall to an index of 84 while the import bill rises with import prices.
Earnings drop below spending: $42.0bn against $55.0bn, a deficit of $13.0bn.

chains.title: From different opportunity costs to a shared gain
steps: Each country divides one output maximum by the other to find what a good costs it: cloth costs Merida 2 grain and Kalto 1.
The country giving up less of the other good has the comparative advantage and moves resources towards that good.
Specialisation is partial, so one good is held constant: cloth stays at 50 and grain rises to 100.
The goods are exchanged at a rate between the two domestic costs — 1.50 grain per cloth.
Each country ends with 10 more grain and no less cloth than it had alone.

chains.title: How a productivity gain removes a reason to trade
steps: Kalto's grain capacity doubles to 80, leaving cloth at 40.
Its opportunity cost of cloth falls to 2 grain.
That is exactly Merida's cost, so neither country gives up less than the other for either good.
With identical opportunity costs there is no comparative advantage and no gain left to divide, so the trade has no basis.
The theory of comparative advantage states that countries should specialise in producing goods where they have the lowest opportunity cost, even if they lack an absolute advantage.
By specialising according to comparative advantage and trading, both countries can consume beyond their production possibility frontiers — total world output increases.
Specialisation leads to higher productivity, economies of scale and more efficient resource allocation, raising real GDP and living standards in trading nations.
The gains from trade include lower prices for consumers, greater product variety, access to resources unavailable domestically and competitive pressure that drives innovation.
chains.title: Comparative advantage shows gains from trade
chains.result: Comparative advantage demonstrates that free trade is mutually beneficial, enabling countries to consume beyond their domestic production capabilities.

steps: A tariff is a tax on imported goods that raises the domestic price above the world price, protecting domestic producers from foreign competition.
The higher price reduces consumer surplus as consumers pay more and consume less, while domestic producers gain surplus by producing more at the higher price.
The government gains tariff revenue on remaining imports, but the net welfare effect is negative — two welfare loss triangles represent the production inefficiency and consumption loss.
Tariffs also invite retaliation from trading partners, potentially triggering trade wars that reduce global trade volumes and harm all participating economies.
chains.title: Tariffs create welfare loss and reduce welfare
chains.result: Tariffs create net welfare losses by raising prices above efficient levels, and risk escalating into destructive trade wars through retaliation.

steps: Trading blocs such as customs unions and free trade areas eliminate tariffs between member states, while maintaining common or individual external tariffs against non-members.
Trade creation occurs when bloc membership shifts production from high-cost domestic producers to lower-cost member state producers, improving allocative efficiency.
Trade diversion occurs when the common external tariff shifts imports from the lowest-cost world producer (outside the bloc) to a higher-cost member state producer.
The net welfare effect depends on the balance between trade creation and trade diversion — blocs are beneficial if trade creation dominates, harmful if diversion dominates.
chains.title: Trading blocs create trade creation and diversion
chains.result: Trading blocs generate both trade creation (efficiency-improving) and trade diversion (efficiency-reducing), with the net effect depending on relative magnitudes.

evaluation.title: An improvement in the terms of trade is not necessarily good news
evaluation.content: Each unit of exports buys more imports, which raises the purchasing power of a given export volume — Sarova's rose to 1.09 units of imports for one of exports. But the higher price is met with smaller orders. With a price elasticity of demand of 1.50, a 20% price rise costs 30% of the volume, leaving an export revenue index of 84 and a trade deficit of $13.0bn. The judgement turns on elasticity and on what caused the movement: an improvement produced by rising domestic inflation is a different proposition from one produced by strong world demand for what the country sells.

evaluation.title: Comparative advantage is a weaker guide to policy than it looks
evaluation.content: The theory predicts a gain of 20 units of output and says nothing about who gets it. The split depends entirely on the exchange rate between the goods, and any rate between 1 and 2 is consistent with the theory — including rates that leave one country with almost nothing. Transport costs come out of the gain before it is shared; rising costs of production mean the advantage runs out before the resources do; and the workers in the industry that closes bear an adjustment cost the national total conceals. None of this removes the gain, but a policy argument that cites the theory without them has cited half of it.

evaluation.title: A pattern of trade is not a fixed feature of a country
evaluation.content: Comparative advantage is a ratio, and ratios move: a country that doubles its productivity in one good can find its opportunity costs converging with its trading partner's, at which point the basis for the trade between them disappears entirely. Emerging economies moving from 24% to 44% of world exports did not find an advantage; investment, education and infrastructure built one. The policy implication is that a country can act on its pattern of trade rather than only respond to it — and that a country resting on an advantage it once had is the one most exposed.

evaluation.title: Comparative advantage has limitations as a guide to policy
evaluation.content: The theory assumes constant opportunity costs, perfect factor mobility within countries, zero transport costs and no externalities. In reality, dynamic comparative advantages can be created through industrial policy and investment in human capital. Countries that follow static comparative advantage may be locked into low-value primary production, while those that develop new industries through strategic intervention may achieve higher long-run growth.

evaluation.title: Infant industry protection may be justified in some cases
evaluation.content: Developing countries may need temporary protection for nascent industries that cannot yet compete with established foreign rivals. Tariffs give domestic firms time to develop economies of scale, learning-by-doing and technological capabilities. However, infant industry protection is often captured by politically connected firms, and 'temporary' protection frequently becomes permanent, reducing long-run efficiency and consumer welfare.

evaluation.title: Trading blocs may undermine global free trade
evaluation.content: While trading blocs promote free trade among members, they maintain barriers against non-members, creating a discriminatory trading system. The proliferation of overlapping bilateral and regional agreements creates a 'spaghetti bowl' of complex rules of origin and regulatory requirements. The WTO's multilateral approach to trade liberalisation may be undermined if countries pursue preferential arrangements rather than global negotiations.
